title: Chapter VIII
paragraphs: On a fine June morning my first lovely little charge was born, the last of the old Earnshaw line. We were haymaking in a distant field when the girl who usually brought our breakfast came running across the meadow and up the lane an hour early, calling to me as she ran.

“Oh, what a grand baby!” she gasped. “The finest lad that ever drew breath! But the doctor says the mistress won’t live: she’s had consumption for months and months. I heard him tell Mr. Hindley. Now there’s nothing to keep her alive, and she’ll be dead before winter. You must come straight home. You’re to nurse him, Nelly, feed him sugar and milk, and care for him night and day. I wish I was you, because he’ll be all yours when there’s no mistress!”
“Is she really so ill?” I asked, dropping my rake and fastening my bonnet.

“I suppose so, though she looks fine,” the girl answered. “And she talks as if she expects to see him grow into a man. She’s beside herself with happiness, he’s so beautiful! If I were her, I’m sure I wouldn’t die. Just looking at him would make me better, whatever Kenneth says. I was quite furious with him. Dame Archer brought the little angel downstairs to the master, and his face had only begun to brighten when the old prophet of doom stepped up. ‘Earnshaw,’ he says, ‘it’s a blessing your wife has lived to leave you this son. I was sure when she arrived that we wouldn’t keep her long; and now I must tell you that winter will probably finish her. Don’t grieve and worry too much: there’s no help for it. Besides, you ought to have known better than to choose a girl as frail as a rush!’”
“What did the master say to that?” I asked.

“I think he cursed, but I wasn’t listening; I was trying to get a look at the baby.” And she began praising him ecstatically again. Just as eager myself, I hurried home to admire him too, though I felt deeply sorry for Hindley. His heart had room for only two idols, his wife and himself: he was devoted to both and worshipped one. I could not imagine how he would endure losing her.
When we reached Wuthering Heights he was standing at the front door. As I went inside, I asked how the baby was.
“Almost ready to run around, Nell!” he answered, forcing a cheerful smile.
“And the mistress?” I ventured. “The doctor says she’s—”

“Damn the doctor!” he broke in, turning red. “Frances is perfectly all right. She’ll be completely well this time next week. Are you going up? Tell her I’ll come if she promises not to talk. I left because she wouldn’t hold her tongue, and she must. Tell her Mr. Kenneth says she must keep quiet.”

I took the message to Mrs. Earnshaw. She seemed giddy with high spirits and answered merrily, “I’ve hardly said a word, Ellen, and he’s gone out crying twice. Well, tell him I promise not to speak; but that doesn’t mean I can’t laugh at him!”

Poor soul! Her cheerful heart never failed her until the last week of her life, and her husband stubbornly—indeed, furiously—insisted that she grew healthier every day. When Kenneth warned him that medicine was useless at this stage of her illness and that further visits would merely add to his expense, Hindley retorted, “I know you needn’t come—she’s well—she doesn’t need any more of your attendance! She never had consumption. It was a fever, and it’s gone. Her pulse is as slow as mine now and her cheek as cool.”

He told his wife the same thing, and she appeared to believe it. But one night, leaning against his shoulder and saying she thought she could get up the next day, she began coughing—a very slight attack. He raised her in his arms; she put both hands round his neck, her face altered, and she was dead.

As the girl had predicted, little Hareton became entirely my responsibility. So long as Mr. Earnshaw saw him healthy and never heard him crying, he was satisfied where the child was concerned. As for himself, he became desperate: his was a grief that would not mourn. He neither prayed nor wept, but cursed and defied, railing against God and humanity and surrendering himself to reckless excess. The servants could not long endure his cruel, tyrannical behaviour; only Joseph and I agreed to remain. I could not bear to leave the child in my care. Besides, as you know, I had been Hindley’s foster sister and excused his conduct more readily than a stranger would. Joseph stayed to bully the tenants and labourers, and because he felt called to remain wherever there was plenty of wickedness to rebuke.

The master’s bad habits and bad company set a fine example for Catherine and Heathcliff. His treatment of Heathcliff could have turned a saint into a devil; and truly, at that time the boy seemed as though something devilish _had_ possessed him. He enjoyed watching Hindley degrade himself beyond redemption, and grew more conspicuous every day for savage sullenness and ferocity. I couldn’t half describe what a hellish house ours was. The curate stopped visiting, and eventually no respectable person came near, unless Edgar Linton’s calls on Miss Cathy counted as an exception. At fifteen she ruled the countryside without a rival, and what a proud, headstrong creature she became! I admit I did not like her after her earliest childhood and often annoyed her by trying to lower her pride. She never disliked me for it, though. She clung wonderfully to old affections: even Heathcliff’s place in her heart stayed unchanged, and young Linton, with all his advantages, struggled to make an equally deep impression. He became my late master. That’s his portrait over the fireplace. It used to hang on one side with his wife’s on the other, but hers has been taken away, or you could see something of what she was like. Can you make him out?

Mrs. Dean lifted the candle, and I saw a gentle-featured face very like the young woman’s at the Heights, though its expression was more thoughtful and kindly. It was a lovely picture. Long fair hair curled a little at the temples; the eyes were large and serious; the figure almost excessively graceful. I could understand Catherine Earnshaw forgetting her first friend for such a man. What astonished me was that he, with a mind presumably matching his appearance, could be attracted to the Catherine Earnshaw I imagined.
“A very pleasing portrait,” I remarked to the housekeeper. “Does it resemble him?”
“Yes,” she said, “but he looked better when something interested him. That’s his ordinary expression: usually he lacked liveliness.”

Catherine had continued seeing the Lintons after her five-week stay. Among them she had no temptation to reveal her rough side, and enough sense to be ashamed of rudeness when they treated her with unfailing courtesy. Her skilful warmth unconsciously deceived the old gentleman and lady, won Isabella’s admiration, and captured her brother’s heart and soul. These conquests flattered her from the beginning—she was full of ambition—and led her to assume two different characters without quite intending to deceive anybody. In the place where she heard Heathcliff called a “vulgar young ruffian” and “worse than a brute,” she took care not to behave like him. At home, though, she felt little desire to practise manners people would only laugh at, or to curb a wilful nature when doing so would win neither praise nor credit.

Mr. Edgar rarely found the courage to visit Wuthering Heights openly. Earnshaw’s reputation frightened him, and he dreaded meeting him. Yet we always did our best to receive him politely. The master himself avoided offending him, knowing why he came, and kept out of sight when he could not be pleasant. I rather think Catherine disliked having Edgar there. She was not scheming, never played the flirt, and clearly objected to her two friends meeting at all. When Heathcliff spoke contemptuously of Linton to his face, she could not agree nearly as readily as when he was absent; and when Linton showed disgust and dislike for Heathcliff, she dared not dismiss his feelings as though contempt for her playmate hardly mattered to her. I often laughed at her perplexities and unspoken troubles, which she tried vainly to hide from my mockery. That sounds unkind, but she was so proud that I found it impossible to pity her until suffering had made her humbler. In the end she did confess and confide in me: there was nobody else she could turn into an adviser.

One afternoon Mr. Hindley went out, and Heathcliff took the liberty of giving himself a holiday because of it. I think he was sixteen then. Neither ugly nor unintelligent, he nevertheless managed to seem repulsive both inside and out, in a way his present appearance gives no trace of. For one thing, he had by then lost the benefit of his early schooling. Endless hard work from early morning until late had extinguished whatever curiosity for knowledge and love of books or learning he once had. The childhood sense of superiority encouraged by old Mr. Earnshaw’s favour had disappeared. He had struggled for a long time to keep pace with Catherine’s studies, surrendering at last with deep, unspoken regret; but his surrender was complete. Once he saw that he must fall below his former level, nobody could persuade him to take even one step towards improving himself. His appearance declined with his mind: he acquired a slouching walk and an undignified look. His naturally reserved character grew into an almost senseless extreme of sullen withdrawal, and he seemed to take grim pleasure in inspiring disgust rather than respect in the few people he knew.

He and Catherine were still constant companions whenever his work allowed, but he no longer put his affection into words. He recoiled from her girlish embraces with angry suspicion, as though sure that giving such affection to him could bring her no pleasure. On the afternoon I mentioned he came inside to announce that he meant to do nothing, while I was helping Miss Cathy arrange her dress. She had not expected him to decide on idleness. Supposing she would have the house to herself, she had somehow let Mr. Edgar know that her brother was away and was preparing to receive him.
“Have you anything to do this afternoon, Cathy?” Heathcliff asked. “Are you going out somewhere?”
“No, it’s raining,” she replied.
“Then why are you wearing that silk dress?” he asked. “I hope nobody’s coming here?”
“Not as far as I know,” Miss stammered. “But you ought to be in the field, Heathcliff. Dinner was an hour ago; I thought you’d left.”
“Hindley doesn’t often spare us his damned presence,” the boy observed. “I’ve finished working for today. I’m staying with you.”
“Oh, but Joseph will report you,” she suggested. “You’d better leave!”
“Joseph’s loading lime beyond Penistone Crags. That’ll keep him busy until dark, and he’ll never find out.”

He strolled over to the fire and sat down. Catherine thought for a moment, frowning; she needed to prepare him for an interruption. After a minute’s silence she said, “Isabella and Edgar Linton mentioned visiting this afternoon. With this rain I don’t really expect them, but they might come, and if they do you’ll have risked a scolding for nothing.”
“Tell Ellen to say you’re busy, Cathy,” he insisted. “Don’t send me away for those pathetic, foolish friends! Sometimes I’m close to complaining that they—but I won’t—”

“That they what?” Catherine asked, looking at him uneasily. “Oh, Nelly!” she added irritably, jerking her head out of my hands. “You’ve combed every curl out of my hair! That’s enough; leave it alone. What are you close to complaining about, Heathcliff?”

“Nothing. Just look at the calendar on the wall.” He pointed to a framed sheet near the window and went on, “Crosses mean evenings you’ve spent with the Lintons, dots mean evenings with me. See? I’ve marked every day.”
“Yes, how silly—as though I kept count!” Catherine replied peevishly. “What sense is there in doing that?”
“It shows that _I_ keep count,” Heathcliff answered.

“Am I supposed to sit with you all the time?” she demanded, more irritated now. “What do I gain from it? What do you talk about? For all you say to entertain me, or all you do either, you might be speechless, or a baby!”
“You’ve never told me before that I didn’t talk enough, or that you didn’t enjoy my company, Cathy!” Heathcliff exclaimed, deeply shaken.
“People who know nothing and say nothing aren’t company at all,” she muttered.

He stood up, but had no chance to say more about his feelings. A horse’s hoofs sounded on the paving stones, and after a gentle knock young Linton entered, his face radiant with pleasure at the unexpected invitation. Catherine must surely have noticed the difference between her friends as one came in and the other went out. It was like leaving bleak, hilly coal country for a beautiful, fertile valley. His greeting and voice were as different as his appearance. He spoke softly and pleasantly, pronouncing his words as you do, less roughly than we speak here and more gently.
“I haven’t arrived too early, have I?” he asked, glancing at me. I had begun polishing the silver and straightening drawers at the far end of the dresser.
“No,” Catherine replied. “Nelly, what are you doing over there?”
“My work, Miss,” I answered. Mr. Hindley had instructed me to act as a third person whenever Linton made a private visit.
She came behind me and whispered angrily, “Take yourself and your dusters away. When guests are here, servants don’t start scrubbing and cleaning the room they’re in!”
“It’s a convenient time, with the master out,” I replied aloud. “He hates me fussing with these things while he’s here. I’m sure Mr. Edgar won’t mind.”
“I hate you fussing while _I’m_ here,” the young lady declared imperiously, giving her visitor no time to answer. She had still not recovered her composure after the small quarrel with Heathcliff.
“I’m sorry to hear that, Miss Catherine,” I answered, and continued working with great diligence.

Thinking Edgar could not see, she snatched the cloth away and gave my arm a long, spiteful, twisting pinch. As I’ve said, I did not love her and rather enjoyed humbling her vanity sometimes; besides, she hurt me badly. I jumped up from my knees and cried out, “Oh, Miss, what a nasty thing to do! You have no right to pinch me, and I won’t stand it.”
“I never touched you, you liar!” she shouted, her fingers itching to do it again and her ears red with fury. She could never conceal her temper; it always set her entire face aflame.
“Then what’s this?” I retorted, displaying a plainly purple witness against her denial.
She stamped, hesitated a moment, then yielded irresistibly to the naughty impulse inside her and slapped my cheek. The sting brought tears to both my eyes.
“Catherine, darling! Catherine!” Linton intervened, horrified at the two offences, lying and violence, his idol had committed.
“Get out of the room, Ellen!” she said again, shaking from head to foot.

Little Hareton, who followed me everywhere and had been sitting beside me on the floor, saw my tears and began crying too. His sobbed complaints about “wicked aunt Cathy” drew her anger onto his unfortunate head. She caught his shoulders and shook him until the poor child went pale, and Edgar, without thinking, seized her hands to free him. Instantly she twisted one hand loose, and the astonished young man felt it strike his ear with a force nobody could mistake for a joke. He recoiled in dismay. I picked Hareton up and carried him to the kitchen, leaving the connecting door open because I wanted to see how they settled their quarrel. The insulted guest, pale and with a trembling lip, moved towards the place where he had left his hat.
“Quite right!” I thought. “Take the warning and leave! It’s a kindness to show you a glimpse of her true character.”
“Where do you think you’re going?” Catherine demanded, moving towards the door.
He turned sideways and tried to get past.
“You can’t go!” she exclaimed forcefully.
“I have to, and I will!” he answered quietly.
“No,” she insisted, seizing the handle. “Not yet, Edgar Linton. Sit down. You aren’t leaving me in that mood. I’d be miserable the whole night, and I refuse to be miserable over you!”
“How can I stay when you’ve hit me?” Linton asked.
Catherine said nothing.
“You’ve made me frightened of you and ashamed of you,” he continued. “I won’t visit you again!”
Her eyes grew shiny, and her eyelids began to flutter.
“And you deliberately told a lie!” he added.
“I didn’t!” she cried, finding her voice. “I didn’t do anything deliberately. Well, go if you like—get out! Now I’ll cry—I’ll make myself ill with crying!”
She sank to her knees beside a chair and began weeping in earnest. Edgar kept to his decision as far as the yard, then lingered there. I decided to encourage him.
“Miss is terribly wilful, sir,” I called. “As bad as any spoiled child. You’d better ride home, or she’ll make herself sick just to upset us.”

The soft-hearted creature cast a sideways glance through the window. He had as much ability to leave as a cat has to abandon a half-dead mouse or a half-eaten bird. Ah, I thought, there’s no saving him: he’s doomed and rushes straight to his fate! So it proved. He turned suddenly, hurried back inside and closed the door. When I went in a little later to warn them that Earnshaw had come home raging drunk, ready to tear the place down round our ears—his usual state of mind when drunk—I saw that the quarrel had only brought them closer. It had broken through the outer defences of youthful shyness and allowed them to drop their disguise of friendship and admit they were lovers.

News of Mr. Hindley’s return sent Linton quickly to his horse and Catherine to her bedroom. I went to hide little Hareton and remove the shot from the master’s hunting gun. In his mad excitement he liked to play with it, endangering anyone who irritated him or merely caught too much of his attention. I had devised the plan of unloading it so that, if he went as far as firing, he might do less harm.
